THE_QUESTION_ANSWERED.asked: why does BringFido display ~122 Indianapolis hotels while PetTripFinder has 67 live pet-friendly and 81 projected?
THE_QUESTION_ANSWERED.answer: because the two numbers count different things, and neither is a coverage gap of the size it appears.
the_arithmetic: BringFido's 122 is the number of properties in its hotel cohort whose city string is literally 'Indianapolis'. Its paginated hotel cohort actually serves 169 properties across the wider market.
Of those 169, 111 are ALREADY Atlas census identities, bound on premises or telephone.
10 are not hotels at all -- two are Airbnb/VRBO category landing pages, two are bed & breakfasts and six are apartment or whole-house rentals.
6 sit outside the Atlas market boundary, four of them in the Zionsville corridor the market contract excludes by name.
3 are BringFido listing the same building twice.
24 are same-brand same-city rows that need an address adjudication before anyone can say whether they are new.
15 are genuine true-missing candidates, of which exactly 1 has been verified first-party in this order.
Atlas's census of 263 is 56% LARGER than BringFido's entire 169-row hotel inventory. Atlas does not know fewer hotels. It publishes fewer, because it publishes only what it has verified first-party.
THE_QUESTION_ANSWERED.the_real_gap: at most 15 identities, not 55 and not the 122-minus-67 the headline suggests. And the gap between 67 published and 263 known is a POLICY-EVIDENCE gap, not a discovery gap: 159 census rows are unresolved because their operative pet policy has never been read from a first-party surface, not because the hotels are unknown.
THE_QUESTION_ANSWERED.do_not_confuse: a competitor's hotel COUNT with new PET-FRIENDLY hotels. BringFido asserts pet-friendliness for every row it lists; Atlas asserts it only with a citable first-party quote.

bringfido.capture_completeness: complete for the hotel surface; pagination walked to exhaustion
capture_defect_found_in_the_competitor: its type filter is inert as a query parameter -- ?type=hotels, ?type=campgrounds and ?type=rentals return byte-identical results. The real filter is a path segment.
its unfiltered lodging page claims '248 pet friendly hotels in Indianapolis' while serving vacation rentals and campgrounds under that label.
5.9% of its own hotel category is not a hotel.

reverse_direction.reading: BringFido misses 10 hotels Atlas has already published as pet-friendly, and lists 3 that Atlas has proven refuse pets with a citable first-party refusal. The competitor is neither a superset nor an authority.

first_party_verification.why_only_one: the attended budget went to proving the brand-inventory technique end to end on one candidate rather than half-proving fifteen. The chain BringFido lead -> Hilton official inventory -> Hilton first-party property page -> publication-grade policy is now demonstrated and repeatable; the remaining 14 are a free-lane backlog.

marriott_hilton.marriott: NOT SWEPT -- recorded as owed, not claimed
marriott_hilton.the_largest_free_opportunity_found: up to 18 unrouted Atlas Hilton rows may be routable from a free brand surface with no provider spend

atlas_coverage.note: the projection is UNCHANGED by this order at 81/44. The one verified hotel is a census admission awaiting a founder ruling, not an application to an existing row.

explained_by: 10 of BringFido's rows are not hotels
3 are duplicate listings of a building already counted
24 require an address adjudication before they can be called new
15 are true-missing candidates, 1 verified so far
and the remainder are Atlas identities that ARE known but whose policy has not been read first-party, which is an evidence gap rather than a discovery gap
explained_difference.geography_is_not_equal: BringFido's 122 counts a city string while the Atlas market is a corridor set that both includes suburbs BringFido files elsewhere and excludes Zionsville, which BringFido includes. The two footprints are not the same shape and no equal-geography claim is made.

cost.note: BringFido refuses an ordinary static GET with 403; the whole capture was done through attended Chrome and same-origin fetch, and no paid lane was touched

should_this_become_a_standard_factory_la.verdict: YES, but as an AUDIT lane, not an acquisition lane
should_this_become_a_standard_factory_la.why: as an acquisition lane it is poor: 169 leads yielded 1 verified pet-friendly hotel, roughly 0.8 per hour, well below the free static and attended lanes this market has already run. As an AUDIT lane it is excellent and cheap: for zero spend it proved the Atlas census is 56% larger than the competitor's inventory, found 3 properties the competitor calls pet-friendly that Atlas has disproven, found 10 non-hotels inside the competitor's hotel category, and bounded the true discovery gap at 15 identities. Knowing the gap is small is worth more than the one hotel it produced.

compare.google_places: exhausted for this market -- 96 of 100 unrouted rows already bought, 91 unbound
compare.firecrawl: exhausted -- 22 rows permanently unreachable; it cost 17 credits for 7 rows
compare.ordinary_unresolved_routing: still the best yield per hour in this market, and the brand-inventory technique found up to 18 more routes for free

regression.why: four artifacts classify UNCLASSIFIED, and the census report's filename additionally trips the *_census_*.json rule as AUTHORITY_CHANGE + ROUTING_SEMANTIC_CHANGE. That classification is stricter than the file deserves -- it is a report, not a census -- but renaming a file to escape a change class is precisely the gaming the order forbids, so the matrix was obeyed as written.
regression.one_run_answered_five_questions: the full suite is a superset of the four required lanes; it was run once and each lane read out of it by node id
